extracted.intended_audience: scientists and scientifically literate readers interested in astronomy/planetary formation (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century scientific essay that advances a dynamical theory for the formation of planets, satellites, rings and nebulae, using hypothetical experiments, physical laws and observational examples to argue for a resisting medium and collision-driven nebula production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a resisting medium for nebular hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: That the nebular hypothesis fails to account for the present condition of the solar system, without the additional hypothesis of a resisting medium in space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues by example (Mars's satellite) that orbits must have contracted since formation and that contraction requires a resisting medium; no other hypothesis seems competent to produce the observed orbital contraction. Surrounding explanation includes how contraction of satellite and planetary orbits follows from such a medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resisting medium and the fate of the universe
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a resisting medium tends to bring the solar and all other systems to a state of quiescence, it has no such tendency on the material universe as a whole, provided the ponderable matter be of infinite extent; if the ponderable matter be of finite extent, it should come to rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the apparent paradox with conservation of force: a resisting medium acting locally causes contraction, but an infinite distribution of matter prevents universal quiescence because radiated energy cannot be lost to 'outer realms.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tidal-disruption criterion for nebulous satellites
rubrics_metrics.description: If a nebulous satellite revolved around a primary in the short period in which most solid satellites now do, the tidal energy generated would be sufficient to tear it into atoms; such a nebulous satellite would be disrupted into a stable nebulous ring and could not reconvert to globular form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by imaginary experiments (icy globe/water globe) showing tidal energy vs internal gravity/cohesion: small nebulous globes rotating too rapidly will be torn apart. Examples compute distances/times for disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law: disruptive ability scales with diameter^3 and period^-2
rubrics_metrics.description: The disruptive ability of the tidal energy of a primary planet on a nebulous satellite of small but unvarying mass varies directly as the cube of the diameter and inversely as the square of the periodic time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This law is explicitly stated and then applied quantitatively (e.g., 10-mile globe in a 100-mile nebulous state yields density estimate and limits on minimum safe rotational period). Used to derive shortest times for a satellite of given density to avoid disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference that solid satellites/planets formed much farther out
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of tidal disruption limits, most solid satellites (and planets) must have been much farther from the center of the system when they condensed from nebulous rings than they are now (example: Mars's nearest satellite must have been at least ~17.5 times its present distance when formed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies the disruptive-law calculations to show required initial orbital radii and concludes that orbits must have contracted since formation, supporting the resisting-medium hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative method: hypothetical physical experiments and order-of-magnitude estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of thought experiments and concrete numerical examples (e.g., icy globe of ten miles, tidal pull causing 160 inches movement in first minute) to illustrate dynamical principles and compare tidal energy to gravity/cohesion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author repeatedly uses simplified examples, assumed densities and periods to make the dynamical arguments concrete and to derive scaling relations; these computations function as methodological criteria for evaluating plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism of planet and satellite formation from contracting nebulous spheroid
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Laplace: a rotating nebulous sphere contracts, flattens, leaves off equatorial rings; radiation and contraction cause agglomeration of particles into nebulous planetoids which coalesce into planets and secondaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise account: slow initial rotation, radiation-driven contraction, formation of an equatorial belt that becomes rings and planetoids, coalescence of planetoids into larger masses, and subsequent development of satellites from out-left rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direction of rotation inherited from accreting planetoids
rubrics_metrics.description: A newly-formed nebulous planet will be given a motion of rotation in the same direction as that of its primary because outer planetoids have greater virtual velocity and impart impulses on coalescence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via momentum/velocity changes when outer and inner planetoids coalesce with the controlling mass; used to justify common direction of rotation in planetary systems absent external disturbance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of external disturbance as exception (asteroids, Uranus)
rubrics_metrics.description: External disturbances (e.g., meteoric/cometary impact or passing bodies) can prevent a ring from collecting into a single mass, explaining exceptions like the asteroid belt and irregularities in Uranus's satellite system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as explanation for observed deviations from the general formation rule; suggests consideration of external perturbations when evaluating formation histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of orbital contraction and possible 'rejuvenation' of systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Contraction due to resisting medium seems to expend life-giving energy, but systems may store potential energy or be reinvigorated by later collisions (e.g., star-star collisions creating new nebulous matter that can form new planetary systems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author traces solar system history from nebulous state to quiescence and describes how collisions between stars could convert kinetic energy to expansive nebulae that seed future systems; this functions as a criterion for assessing long-term cosmical evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modus operandi of conservation: stellar collisions produce expanding nebulae and expelled masses
rubrics_metrics.description: When stars (or cooled planets) meet with high velocities, the heat generated will expand the combined mass into nebulous vapor, and much of this mass may be thrown beyond the sphere of attraction, becoming comets, meteoric showers, or material for other systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author quantifies expected velocities and heat (example velocities ~400–500 miles/sec producing enormous temperatures), divides expanding mass into inner/outer parts to argue how some mass becomes ejected to surrounding stars; used to explain observed novae and supply material for cosmical dust/asteroids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected near-uniform density of newly-formed nebulae after explosion
rubrics_metrics.description: At the moment after the expansive force has expended its last effort, the resultant nebula must be of very nearly uniform density due to the outward motions of particles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is offered as a diagnostic expectation for freshly produced nebulae and informs interpretation of observational spectra and morphological evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational confirmation via temporary stars (novae) and spectral changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Explosions/collisions that produce nebulae have been observed as temporary stars (novae) with characteristic spectral evolution (initial rainbow-tinted continuous spectrum due to intense pressure, later showing 'spectrum of a true nebula'); cited examples include May 1866 event and the new star in Cygnus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author points to spectral analysis (hydrogen emission, changes over time) and historical records (Herschel, Proctor) as empirical support; thus, reproducing the spectral sequence is a test for the collision/nebula hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite vs infinite ponderable matter: long-term dynamical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If the ponderable moving matter of the universe is limited, repeated collisions will convert motion into heat and radiate it away leaving ponderable matter to collect and cool into quiescence; if matter is infinite, there are no outer realms to lose motion and motion can continue forever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a cosmological criterion: whether one expects ultimate heat-death/quiescence or perpetual motion depends on global matter extent; the argument ties local dynamical mechanisms to cosmic-scale expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satellites absorption via ring decay and planetary accretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Planets absorb their satellites by first converting them into fragmentary rings which approach and fall upon planetary surfaces, becoming part of them; likewise planets approach primaries and are absorbed in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a mechanism for gradual decay of satellite systems and eventual approach to quiescence; relevant for interpreting ring systems (e.g., Saturn) and the long-term evolution of planetary systems.
